e.t: Abiezek, also rendered Aviezek, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at 1 Samuel 11:8. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, its precise referent cannot be stated, but the word’s basic function is clear: it serves as a personal or place name in that passage.

This adverb means “unceasingly”: it describes an action or condition that continues without stopping or interruption. It answers the question “how?” by showing that something is done continually rather than only once or occasionally. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs six times, all in deuterocanonical books, especially 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any sentence depends on the action it modifies, but its central idea remains steady continuation.

Akor is a proper name, rendered simply as “Akor.” In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 2:27. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not state whether Akor refers to a person, place, or another named subject. Its precise significance in that verse therefore depends on the surrounding passage and the person or subject being named there.

This noun means “thoughtlessness” or “rashness”: acting without careful consideration or sound judgment. It describes a careless, impulsive quality rather than a deliberate decision. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Its ordinary sense points to behavior marked by insufficient reflection, especially when caution and wise judgment are needed. “Thoughtlessness” is also the attested English rendering for one occurrence, agreeing with the central meaning of the word.

This noun refers to “vengeance on” or “revenge on”—an act of retaliation directed against someone. It names the response of seeking repayment or punishment for a wrong, rather than describing the person who was wronged. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 5:17. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and larger context.

This Greek LXX verb means “gird up”: to draw clothing or something around the body and secure it. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Judges 18:16 and Proverbs 31:17. Its basic sense is the physical act of fastening or gathering what is worn around oneself. The surrounding verse determines whether the action is presented simply as clothing, movement, or readiness for activity.

This adjective means “man-woman” or “hermaphrodite,” describing someone understood as having both male and female characteristics. It is a descriptive word rather than a personal name or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Proverbs 18:8. The supplied lexical meaning identifies the word’s basic reference, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain how that description functions in its specific setting.

This verb means “stand up; resurrect.” It describes rising from a position and can also express being raised to life again. In this Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 446 times, making it a broadly used action word rather than a rare expression. Its precise force—ordinary physical rising or resurrection—depends on the sentence and surrounding passage. It appears throughout the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented in this Greek corpus.

This verb means to reproach someone or to judge in turn, expressing a direct response in which one person answers another with criticism or judgment. It appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Job, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. The word describes an active verbal response rather than a person, object, or general condition.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “deprived of sight.” It describes a condition in which sight has been taken away or is absent, functioning as an action or state rather than naming a person or object. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Isaiah 44:18. That reference identifies its only occurrence, while the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its specific force in that passage.

This verb means to divide or set apart—to separate something or someone from another. It describes an act of making a distinction or creating separation, rather than merely noticing that things are different. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Joshua and once in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on what is being separated and why, but the central idea remains deliberate division or setting apart.

This verb means “run off”—to leave by running or hurry away from a place. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes physical departure rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. The word occurs 21 times in the LXX corpus, across the Old Testament and once in Sirach. Its exact force in any verse depends on who is leaving and the surrounding passage, but its central picture is a person moving away quickly.

It means “without fire,” describing something that lacks fire or has not been exposed to it. This is an adjective, so it characterizes a person, object, or substance rather than naming an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 13:12. The word’s basic sense is narrow and concrete: it identifies something by the absence of fire. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX preposition means “without,” expressing the absence of a person, thing, or condition. It indicates that something is done or exists apart from what is named. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 12:15. Its basic sense is therefore straightforward: it marks separation from or lack of something, while the surrounding sentence determines exactly what is absent.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Auōth” or “Avoth.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Deuteronomy 3:14. The available information identifies the name and its occurrence, but does not provide enough context to determine whether it refers to a person, place, or another named subject. Its precise reference therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “pain” or “distress”—the experience of suffering, anguish, or trouble. It names an affliction rather than an action, and its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, appearing four times in Old Testament books and once in Sirach. Its occurrences include 1 Samuel, Psalms, and Sirach, showing that it can describe painful human experience across several settings.

Baltasar, also rendered Valtasar, is a personal name rather than a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical material, it identifies a person by name. This proper noun occurs 11 times, especially in Daniel and also in Baruch. Its normal function is simply to name or refer to someone called Baltasar. The supplied references include Daniel 1:7, Daniel 2:26, and several passages in Daniel 5.

Baourim, also given as Vaurim, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament, identifying a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs four times in this LXX corpus, all in four Old Testament verses: three in 2 Samuel and one in 1 Kings. The lexical information gives the name itself but no further descriptive meaning. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

In the Greek LXX, this noun refers to a “countryman” or to “neighborhood women.” It identifies people connected by their local community or nearby surroundings, so its basic sense is relational: it names someone in relation to place and neighbors. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek LXX, across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, including Exodus, Ruth, Job, Psalms, and Jeremiah. Its precise nuance in a particular verse depends on that verse’s surrounding context.

This word means “senate,” referring to an organized council of senior people who share public authority. It is a noun used for a recognized body rather than for one individual. The word occurs 32 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing across the Old Testament and included deuterocanonical books. Its repeated use shows a stable reference to a formal council or assembly with a public role, while the precise responsibility of that senate depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun refers to women’s apartments—the part of a royal or wealthy household where women lived—or, more broadly, a harem. It can describe a group of women associated with one household or ruler rather than simply referring to women in general. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 42 times, showing that it is used across several historical books. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Darda, also called Thartha, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once within this LXX corpus, at 1 Kings 5:11. The available meaning is therefore the person’s name itself; the name does not provide a separate ordinary definition such as a trait or activity. Its precise significance in that passage must come from the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means “confuse”: to unsettle or throw someone into a state of uncertainty. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Habakkuk 2:16, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the act of confusing or disorienting someone.

This Greek LXX noun means a thing torn to pieces, or prey. It refers to something that has been torn apart, especially in the sense of an animal or other spoil taken by force. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at Jeremiah 37:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains something torn apart or seized as prey.

This noun means “roofing,” referring to the material or covering that forms a roof over a building. It names a physical part of a structure rather than an action or personal quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ecclesiastes 10:18. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but the word itself points plainly to roofing as a building covering. This is a narrow, concrete term describing what protects the interior of a house or other structure from above.

This adverb means “if indeed,” expressing a condition with emphasis or confirming that the condition is truly the case. It introduces a statement that depends on something being so, while drawing attention to the reality of that condition. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 3:38; the surrounding verse is needed to explain precisely how the condition functions there.

This noun means “remnant; residue”: what remains after the greater part has been removed, lost, or passed away. It can refer to a remaining portion or to people who are left after others are gone. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, all in Old Testament verses, including passages from Deuteronomy, Ezra, Psalms, and Jeremiah. Its basic meaning is therefore something remaining from an earlier whole, whether a material remainder or a surviving group.

This adjective describes something as being twenty years old or connected with an age of twenty years. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 28 times, always in Old Testament passages, especially in Numbers. Its basic function is precise age description rather than a name for a person or object. The word appears from Exodus through Ezra, showing repeated use when ages or age-based distinctions are stated. Its lexical meaning is simply “of twenty years.”

This LXX conjunction means “whether,” introducing an alternative, uncertainty, or a choice between possibilities. It connects clauses or options rather than naming a person, object, action, or quality. The word occurs nine times across five verses in the LXX corpus, including passages in Joshua, Job, Isaiah, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in a sentence depends on the alternatives or clauses it joins.

This Greek LXX verb means “knock out.” It describes the action of knocking something or someone out, presenting a forceful action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented by the LXX, at Deuteronomy 19:5. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic verbal sense remains the act of knocking out.

This verb describes prostituting oneself or another, and more broadly acting in a depraved way. Its central idea is sexual corruption expressed through conduct. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 44 times, so it is used across multiple passages rather than being limited to one isolated account. The wording can describe a person’s immoral behavior or the corrupting of others, while the surrounding verse determines its precise force.

This adjective describes someone who is “terrified”—overcome by intense fear. It refers to a person’s fearful condition rather than to an action they perform. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in Deuteronomy and once in 1 Maccabees. The central idea remains a strong state of fear, though the surrounding verse determines what caused that fear and how it is expressed.

This word means “mine” or “my own.” It identifies something as belonging to, being possessed by, or being personally associated with someone. As an adjective, it normally describes a person or thing in relation to its owner, distinguishing what belongs to one person from what belongs to another. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 104 times, showing regular use for expressing personal ownership or association. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding words and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “ambush”: to lie in wait and attack someone unexpectedly. It describes a deliberate action rather than a general conflict or open battle. The word occurs 25 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented in this LXX corpus, showing repeated use for concealed attacks and surprise assaults. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains an attack prepared from hiding.

This word means “in arms” or “armed,” describing a person or group equipped for fighting. As an adjective or noun, it can identify those who possess weapons or are prepared for military action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, and each recorded English rendering is “armed.” Its basic sense is therefore direct: being equipped with weapons, or referring to people who are so equipped. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on the condition of being armed or on armed people.

This adjective describes something that is “beyond what is ordained”—outside what has been appointed or prescribed. It functions as a description of an action, condition, or matter that exceeds an established order. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in Job, so its normal use is tied to describing something as surpassing what has been set in place. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being described.

This adjective describes something attractive or tempting—something that draws a person toward it because it appears appealing. It can refer to an enticement or an appealing prospect, while the surrounding sentence determines what is being described. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 8:15. Since no verse text is provided, the word’s exact force in that passage cannot be stated beyond this central sense: it portrays something with the power to attract or entice.

This word means “whenever”. As a particle, it introduces a time or condition that may occur. It marks a circumstance as possible or recurring rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs once, in Bel and the Dragon 1:11. Its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic contribution remains clear: it links what follows with the time or situation in which something happens.

This adjective means “caught,” describing someone or something that has been apprehended or seized. It presents the person or thing as already caught rather than as the one doing the catching. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within three verses: twice in 1 Samuel and once in 2 Kings. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Esebias, also rendered Esevias, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Nehemiah 10:12. The name itself gives the person’s designation, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain that individual’s specific role or significance there.

This adjective describes something that is loud or pleasing to hear. It can point to sound that is strong enough to be noticed, while also carrying the sense of being agreeable or attractive to the ear. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 30:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning concerns the character of a sound—either its volume or the pleasure it gives the listener.

Euila, also rendered Eila, is a proper name referring to a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is a personal designation rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs twice in the Greek form of Genesis: once in Genesis 10:7 and again in Genesis 10:29. The available lexical meaning identifies the name itself, but the name’s particular family or genealogical role must be understood from the surrounding passage in each occurrence.

This word means “nail,” referring to a metal fastening used to secure something in place. As a noun, it can describe nails used in construction or other physical objects, and it can also support figurative descriptions when the surrounding passage gives that force. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times across eight verses, including passages connected with building and with the stability of firmly fixed words. Its exact significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding text.

Thanemath is a proper name used as a specific designation, rather than an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. Its lexical meaning is simply “Thanemath.” In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 25:23. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish whether it refers to a person, place, or another named subject. Its role is therefore to identify a particular named entity in that passage.

Thekeminas is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It is a proper noun in the Greek Old Testament and occurs three times, all in 1 Kings. The name appears in 1 Kings 11:19, 1 Kings 11:20, and 1 Kings 12:24. Since names normally identify people rather than carry a general definition, its basic meaning here is simply the person’s name, Thekeminas.

This Greek Old Testament noun refers to provocation or temper. It can name something that stirs anger or the angry disposition itself, depending on how it is used in a sentence. The word occurs 309 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings preserved in the Septuagint corpus, so it is a well-attested term rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

Iachin, also rendered Iakhin, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies individuals in genealogical and priestly lists rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. The name appears six times in six Old Testament verses, from Genesis through Nehemiah. Its exact significance as a personal name is not explained by the available passages, so the clearest meaning is simply the name itself: Iachin or Iakhin.

Iealē, also given as Ieali, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as an identifying name in the Greek Old Testament, distinguishing someone named in the biblical record. The available information does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain more about the person or group associated with it. This name occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:58.

Iemla is a proper name, used to identify a person rather than to describe an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Septuagint (LXX), it appears four times, in four verses: twice in 1 Kings 22 and twice in 2 Chronicles 18. The name itself is given as “Iemla,” without an additional English definition. Its precise role in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means a fowler, or bird-catcher—someone who captures birds. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Amos, and refers to the person who sets or uses a trap for birds. The word itself identifies the bird-catcher rather than the bird or the trap. Its appearances are in Amos 3:5, 8:1, and 8:2, but the precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “equality,” referring to a state in which people or things are regarded as equal. It is a noun, so it names the condition or principle of being equal rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Job 36:29 and Zechariah 4:7. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning remains the idea of equal standing, measure, or treatment.

This verb means “stand” or “establish.” It can describe being upright or taking a standing position, and it can also express setting something firmly in place or causing it to remain established. The Septuagint uses it broadly, appearing 666 times across its Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact sense depends on whether the sentence focuses on a person’s position or on establishing something securely.

This verb means “fly down,” describing movement from a higher position toward a lower one. It presents the action plainly, without by itself explaining why something descends or what happens afterward. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 43:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains the downward movement of flying.

This word means “spy”: a person sent to observe another place or people, often secretly, in order to bring back information. It is a noun describing the person who carries out this assignment, rather than the act of spying itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Jewish writings represented here, it occurs 10 times, including several passages in Genesis 42 concerning men accused of investigating the land. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “horn,” referring to the horn of an animal or to a horn-shaped object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented by this LXX corpus, it occurs 95 times, from Genesis through 2 Maccabees. The word appears in descriptions involving animals, worship, kingship, and prophetic imagery, but its basic meaning remains horn. The surrounding verse determines whether the reference is literal or figurative.

This proper name refers to “Kitioi; Kiti.” It functions as a name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Genesis 10:4 and once in 1 Chronicles 1:7. Because no surrounding verse text is provided here, the name’s specific reference in each passage must be understood from those genealogical contexts. Its consistent use as a proper name is the central meaning available for this LXX term.

This LXX noun means “hollow,” referring to a hollow place or feature. It functions as a naming word for such a thing, rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 8:14. The word’s basic sense is therefore concise: it identifies a hollow. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This noun means “plaster; stucco,” referring to a material used as a coating or surface covering. It names a physical building substance rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 5:5. The word’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical sense remains the plaster or stucco material itself.

Lebōna, also rendered Levona, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This form occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Judges 21:19, so its ordinary function is identifying a particular name rather than expressing a general vocabulary meaning. The available lexical information does not establish a broader symbolic or descriptive sense.

gl: place where people assembled to talk and hear news; lounge
d: place where people assembled to talk and hear news; lounge

e.t: This word refers to a place where people assembled to talk and hear news—a lounge or gathering place. It is a noun naming a location rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 23:29. Its basic sense is a social setting where people meet and converse. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies a place associated with conversation, news, and communal gathering.

The word means “Magus” and functions as a noun naming a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Daniel chapter 2: Daniel 2:2 and Daniel 2:10. These references locate its uses, but the word’s precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording. As a lexical term, it identifies the person designated by this noun.

This verb describes acting cowardly—showing a lack of courage rather than standing firm. It names an action marked by timidity in the face of difficulty, danger, pressure, or duty. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 6:17. The word itself gives the basic description; the surrounding passage is needed to identify exactly what prompted the cowardice in that verse.

This word is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It is represented as “Masezebēl” or “Masezevil.” In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 3:4. Because it is a name, its ordinary meaning is primarily identification: it tells the reader who a person is, while the surrounding passage supplies that person’s role and significance. No additional lexical definition or contextual description is provided here.

Machiri, also written Makhiri, is a proper name identifying an individual in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship; its meaning is the personal name itself. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Numbers 26:33. Without the verse text and surrounding context, the name alone does not establish additional details about the person or the role connected with him.

This verb means “get drunk”: it describes becoming intoxicated rather than simply drinking. As a verb, it expresses an action or condition someone enters. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it occurs once, at Proverbs 23:31. The word’s basic sense remains focused on drunkenness; its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX verb means “reverse”: to turn something back or cause it to go in the opposite direction. It describes an action of changing a course, movement, or outcome rather than naming a person or object. The word occurs 22 times in the Greek LXX, appearing in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being turned or changed in that surrounding passage.

This verb means to be “wroth with” someone—to hold anger toward that person. It describes an active response of displeasure directed at another, rather than a general condition or feeling with no object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs four times: three times in Old Testament books and once in Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words and passage.

This word means “harp” or “stringed instrument,” referring to a musical instrument used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings. As a noun, it names the instrument itself rather than the act of playing it. It occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages describing groups of musicians and musical worship. The precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This noun means “feeding-place,” referring to a place where nourishment is provided or animals are fed. It is a concrete location word rather than a description of the food itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented here, it occurs 392 times, so its exact reference can depend on the surrounding sentence. The word appears across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical portions of this Greek corpus, while its central sense remains a place associated with feeding.

This noun means “journey,” referring to travel from one place to another. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times: three times in Wisdom and once in 1 Maccabees. Its basic sense is the journey itself rather than a person making the journey or a specific destination. The surrounding wording determines whether the journey is described as ordinary travel or serves a larger purpose in the passage.citep03:word:lxx:L709450:identityp03:word:lxx:L709450:occurrences

This adjective describes someone or something as pitiable—being in a condition that calls for compassion because of a piteous plight. It focuses on the condition of the person or situation, rather than naming an action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs four times: once in Jeremiah and three times in deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in any particular verse is clarified by the surrounding passage.

gl: pledge for the maintenance of unity; surety
d: pledge for the maintenance of unity; surety

e.t: This word refers to a pledge or surety—a person or arrangement that guarantees an agreement and helps preserve unity between parties. As a noun, it names the guarantee itself or the one who stands as security; as an adjective, it can describe something serving that purpose. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs eight times, chiefly in 1 Maccabees and once in Isaiah. Its central idea is dependable assurance that a relationship or agreement will hold together.

Ouiechōa, also rendered Oiekhoa, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it functions as an individual name. This name appears once in the Greek LXX, at Ezra 10:36. The supplied lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the person or the event. Its precise significance in that passage therefore depends on the surrounding context.

This verb means “do” or “go,” describing an action or movement. Depending on the sentence, it can point to carrying something out or to going somewhere. It functions as a verb, so it expresses what someone does or where someone goes rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it is attested once, at Sirach 36:27. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine whether doing or going is intended there.

This adjective describes something belonging to or involving the "whole community," making it "public" rather than private. It points to what is shared openly by the people as a group. In the Greek LXX, the word appears once, in 2 Maccabees 3:18. Its exact force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its ordinary meaning focuses on the entire community and what is publicly known or experienced.

This Greek LXX verb means “order”: it expresses giving a directive or instruction for someone to follow. As a verb, it describes the act of directing rather than the command itself. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, with one occurrence in Proverbs and one in 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is the issuing of an order.

This Greek LXX verb means “sprinkle,” describing the act of scattering or applying small drops or particles over something. It can refer to a physical action involving substances such as dust, liquid, or another material. The word occurs seven times in the Greek LXX corpus, across five Old Testament passages and two deuterocanonical passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being sprinkled and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the deliberate scattering or application of a substance.

This adverb means “near” or “hard by,” describing something located close to another person or place. It expresses nearness rather than distance and normally answers the question of where something is in relation to something else. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 34:2. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains simple: something is close at hand or nearby.

This noun means “scale of a balance,” the weighing instrument used to compare or measure weight. It names a physical tool rather than an action or quality. In this LXX corpus, it occurs twice, once in Wisdom and once in 2 Maccabees. Its basic sense is therefore a tool used for weighing, while the precise force of either occurrence depends on the surrounding verse.

This adjective describes someone or something as gentle—marked by a mild, considerate quality rather than forcefulness. It presents gentleness as a recognizable character or manner, though the precise emphasis depends on the sentence where it appears. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 15:12. Its central meaning remains straightforward: it identifies what is gentle.

This Greek word means “ordain” or “order”: it describes giving an authoritative command, directing something to be done, or establishing an arrangement. As a verb, it focuses on the act of issuing an instruction rather than merely making a request. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 59 times, so it can describe commands or arrangements in many kinds of situations. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on who gives the command and what is being ordered.

This Greek LXX noun means “fold,” referring to something bent over or arranged in a doubled layer. It names the fold itself rather than describing an action. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament portion represented here, in Job 41:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains a fold or layered part of something.

This verb describes something breaking or bursting open with force. It points to a sudden rupture or the act of giving way, rather than a quiet movement. As a verb, it names an action in which something breaks or bursts, rather than describing an object or person. In the Greek Old Testament, the LXX, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 13:13. Its central meaning is “break; burst,” while the surrounding passage determines exactly what is affected.

This noun describes swaying or rocking—the movement of something that shifts back and forth. It presents motion rather than a person, object, or action of speech. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs seven times, appearing in Psalms, Lamentations, Jonah, and Sirach. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being described and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains unsteady back-and-forth movement. The word is preserved in passages ranging from the Psalms to later wisdom literature.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Sebōin” or “Sevin.” It identifies a named person or place rather than describing an action, quality, or ordinary object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Isaiah 45:14. The name’s precise referent and significance depend on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic function is simply to identify the named entity associated with that occurrence.

“Semeΐ; Semi” is a proper name used for people in the Greek Old Testament, not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies individuals named Semei or Semi, with the surrounding passage needed to distinguish which person is intended. The name occurs 46 times in 41 Old Testament verses, from Exodus through Nehemiah. Its appearances include genealogical records and historical narratives, but no broader lexical meaning is supplied for the name itself.

This word means “scorpion,” the venomous creature known for its stinging tail. It is a noun referring to the animal itself, whether one scorpion or more than one. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs 10 times. The word appears in descriptions of wilderness dangers and in comparisons involving harsh treatment, but its basic meaning remains the creature rather than the comparison or lesson drawn from it. The precise force of any particular occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word is the proper name Solomon, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It is the Greek LXX form of the name and is rendered “Solomon.” Within the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 8:7. Since no verse text is provided, the word itself establishes the person’s name, while the surrounding passage supplies the specific role or significance of Solomon in that occurrence.

This verb means “crucify”: to put someone to death by fastening that person to a cross or stake. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs twice, both times in Esther. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning remains the act of crucifying. The word appears in Esther 7:9 and Esther 8:12.

This Greek LXX noun means “equipment,” referring broadly to the gear or supplies prepared for use. It is a practical word for the material things needed to outfit a person, group, or undertaking, rather than an abstract quality or action. Within the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 1–3 Maccabees. The exact force in any one passage depends on what kind of equipment the surrounding verse identifies, but the central idea remains prepared gear or supplies.

This verb means to “commingle” or “compose”: to mix things together so that they form a combined whole. It can describe elements being blended rather than remaining separate. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs twice, once in Daniel and once in 2 Maccabees. The basic idea is joining or combining parts, while the precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject.

This verb means “sew”: to join material by stitching it together. It describes a practical action involving fabric or another material that can be sewn, rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears two times, once in Job and once in Ezekiel. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its ordinary meaning remains the act of sewing or stitching material together.

This Greek LXX adverb means “quickly,” describing an action done rapidly or without delay. It tells how an action occurs rather than naming a person, object, or event. The word appears 31 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, including passages from Genesis, Deuteronomy, Judges, Psalms, Isaiah, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the action and surrounding words, but its central idea remains speed or promptness.

This Greek LXX verb means “healthy,” describing someone or something as being in a sound, well condition. It expresses the state of health rather than naming a person, object, or place. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, so it is used across several passages rather than being limited to one setting. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding words and passage.

This Greek verb means “submit” or “risk.” It describes placing something under another’s authority or putting something at stake, depending on the sentence. It is an action word rather than a name or description. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, it occurs 13 times, so its precise force is determined by what is being submitted or risked and by the surrounding context. The central idea remains an intentional act of placing something under another or exposing it to possible loss.

This adjective describes someone or something as “sparing” or “thrifty,” emphasizing careful use of resources rather than wastefulness. It can characterize a person’s restrained, economical approach or describe conduct marked by prudence in spending or provision. In the Greek LXX corpus, this word occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 2:9. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense concerns economy, restraint, and avoiding unnecessary expenditure.

This Greek LXX noun expresses “character of the.” The phrase is incomplete by itself, so its full reference depends on the surrounding wording in Wisdom 14:18. It does not provide enough information here to identify the person, object, or quality whose character is being described. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Wisdom 14:18. Its basic contribution is to point to character, while “the” connects that description to something named in the surrounding text.

This noun means “nature,” referring to the inherent character, condition, or order belonging to a person, living thing, or part of creation. It can describe what something is like by its own constitution rather than by a temporary appearance or external arrangement. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs 12 times, especially in 4 Maccabees and Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what kind of person, creature, or created reality the surrounding sentence discusses.

This verb means to illuminate or enlighten—to give light or bring understanding. It can describe making something brighter, but it can also express the giving of insight or understanding. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 38 times, appearing across passages from Exodus through the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains bringing light, whether in a visible or understanding-related sense.

This verb means “useful”: it describes something that serves a practical benefit or proves helpful. As a verb, it expresses the idea of being useful rather than naming a person, object, or quality by itself. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it occurs twice, once in Wisdom and once in Sirach. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains usefulness or practical benefit.
